questions.title: Z-score test for a biased-looking measurement result
questions.prompt: A Hadamard-gate circuit is run for 1024 shots and returns 480 counts of "0" (so 544 of "1"). Walk through how you'd test whether this is consistent with the expected p0 = 0.5, compute the z-score, and state whether it passes at 95% and at 99% confidence.
questions.modelAnswer: phat = 480/1024 = 0.46875. SE = sqrt(0.5*0.5/1024) = 0.015625. z = (0.46875 - 0.5)/0.015625 = -2.0. At the 95% confidence level (|z| < 1.96) this fails, since |z| = 2.0 exceeds 1.96 — the result would be flagged as inconsistent with a fair coin. At the 99% confidence level (|z| < 2.58), the same |z| = 2.0 passes. The confidence level has to be chosen and stated before running the test, because the identical data gives opposite verdicts depending on which threshold you commit to.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd say: this is exactly the kind of result that looks borderline until you pin down which confidence level you committed to. At z = -2.0 it fails a 95% check but passes a 99% check, so the honest answer depends entirely on a decision you should have made before looking at the data, not after.
questions.example: assert_consistent_with_expected_p(480, 1024, expected_p=0.5, confidence_z=1.96) raises AssertionError; the same call with confidence_z=2.58 passes.
commonMistakes: Picking the confidence threshold after seeing whether the result passes or fails (post-hoc threshold selection)
Reporting only 'it failed' without stating which confidence level was used
Confusing a failed z-test with proof the hardware is broken, rather than one data point consistent with normal sampling variance at a stricter threshold
keyPoints: SE = sqrt(p0(1-p0)/n) for a binary proportion
z = (phat - p0)/SE
|z| < 1.96 is roughly 95% confidence; |z| < 2.58 is roughly 99%
The confidence level must be chosen and documented before running the test

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct pass/fail verdict at both confidence levels
Explains why the threshold must be pre-committed

questions.title: Chi-square test for a Bell state's outcome distribution
questions.prompt: A Bell state is run for 2000 shots and returns counts {'00': 1013, '11': 987, '01': 0, '10': 0} against an expected {'00': 1000, '11': 1000}. Compute the chi-square statistic and explain how you'd decide whether this result passes at 99% confidence with 1 degree of freedom.
questions.modelAnswer: chi2 = sum((observed-expected)^2/expected) across the nonzero-expected categories: (1013-1000)^2/1000 + (987-1000)^2/1000 = 0.169 + 0.169 = 0.338. With 1 degree of freedom, the chi-square critical value for 99% confidence is 6.63. Since 0.338 is far below 6.63, the result passes comfortably — the observed counts are well within normal sampling variance of the expected 50/50 split between '00' and '11', and the '01'/'10' leakage is exactly zero, which is also expected for an ideal Bell state.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through the chi-square sum term by term so it's auditable, then compare against the critical value rather than eyeballing it — 0.338 against 6.63 isn't close, so this is an easy pass, not a borderline call.
commonMistakes: Including categories with zero expected count in the denominator, causing a division-by-zero or an invalid statistic
Using the wrong degrees of freedom for the number of free categories
Treating a passing chi-square test as proof of a perfect device rather than evidence consistent with the expected distribution at this shot count
keyPoints: chi2 = sum((observed_i - expected_i)^2 / expected_i)
Degrees of freedom here is 1 (two free outcome categories)
Critical value 6.63 at 99% confidence for 1 df
A low chi-square relative to the critical value means the distribution is consistent with expectation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct comparison against the critical value
Explains what a pass does and doesn't prove

questions.title: Why precision scales with the square root of shot count
questions.prompt: Explain the relationship between shot count and measurement precision, and why getting a 10x improvement in precision costs 100x the shots rather than 10x.
questions.modelAnswer: Standard error of a measured expectation value scales as 1/sqrt(shots). At 1,000 shots the relative standard error is about 0.0316; at 4,000 shots (4x) it drops to about 0.0158 — exactly half. Because the relationship is a square root, you must multiply shots by the square of the precision factor you want: a 10x reduction in standard error requires 10^2 = 100x the shots. This is the single most important number for budgeting, because it means chasing 'more precision' has rapidly compounding cost, while most downstream decisions only need a specific, bounded precision target.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always lead with the square-root relationship because it's the one fact that stops people from padding shot counts 'for safety' — doubling precision isn't double the cost, it's quadruple, and that compounds fast once you're asking for an order of magnitude.
questions.example: Going from 500 to 8,000 shots (16x) only cuts relative standard error from 0.0447 to 0.0112 (4x better), illustrating the diminishing returns directly.
commonMistakes: Assuming precision scales linearly with shot count
Not distinguishing the per-task flat fee (which doesn't scale with shots) from the per-shot fee (which does) when estimating cost increase
Setting a shot budget to a round number instead of deriving it from the actual precision the downstream decision needs
keyPoints: Standard error scales as 1/sqrt(shots)
4x shots halves standard error
100x shots gives a 10x precision improvement
Precision targets should be derived from the decision the measurement feeds, not chosen arbitrarily

questions.title: AWS Braket's per-task and per-shot pricing structure
questions.prompt: Explain how AWS Braket prices a quantum job, and compute the total cost of a 200-task, 1,000-shot-per-task job on both IonQ Aria ($0.30/task + $0.03/shot) and OQC Lucy ($0.30/task + $0.00035/shot).
questions.modelAnswer: Braket charges a flat per-task fee plus a per-shot fee that varies by hardware vendor. For 200 tasks at 1,000 shots each (200,000 total shots): IonQ Aria = 200*$0.30 + 200,000*$0.03 = $60 + $6,000 = $6,060.00. OQC Lucy = 200*$0.30 + 200,000*$0.00035 = $60 + $70 = $130.00. That's roughly a 46x cost difference for the identical workload, purely from device choice, before even considering whether each device's qubit count, connectivity, or error rate actually fits the problem.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd run both numbers out loud before saying anything about which device to pick, because the dollar gap is so large it changes the conversation — but I'd immediately follow it with the caveat that cheapest isn't automatically right if the circuit doesn't fit or the queue is long.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the flat per-task fee applies regardless of shot count
Picking the cheapest device without checking qubit count, connectivity, or queue depth
Assuming all vendors on Braket have the same per-shot rate
keyPoints: Braket pricing = per-task fee + (per-shot fee * shots)
Per-shot fee varies dramatically by hardware vendor
IonQ Aria: $6,060 vs OQC Lucy: $130 for the identical workload
Cost is one input to backend selection, not the only one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Notes cost isn't the only selection factor

questions.title: IBM Quantum's runtime-second billing vs. Braket's shot-based billing
questions.prompt: Explain why you can't compare an IBM Quantum Pay-As-You-Go quote directly against an AWS Braket quote just by looking at shot counts, and compute IBM's cost for a job estimated to take 240 seconds at $1.60/billable second.
questions.modelAnswer: IBM's Pay-As-You-Go plan bills by wall-clock runtime second, not by task or shot count. Cost = 240 seconds * $1.60/sec = $384.00. Braket's cost depends on shots and tasks directly; IBM's depends on how long the job actually runs, which is itself a function of circuit depth and provider-counted queueing/execution behavior, not shot count alone. Two jobs with identical shot counts can have very different IBM runtime costs if their circuits differ in depth, so you can't translate a Braket shot-based quote into an IBM quote without first estimating runtime seconds.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mistake I watch for is someone assuming shot count is a universal cost unit across providers — it isn't. IBM's dimension is time, so the estimation step itself (runtime, not shots) is where the real work is before you can even compare the two quotes.
commonMistakes: Assuming shot count directly translates into cost on every provider
Ignoring that circuit depth and queueing behavior affect IBM's billable runtime
Comparing a Braket shot-based number to an IBM runtime-based number without converting either to a common basis
keyPoints: IBM bills by runtime-second, not by shot or task
Runtime depends on circuit depth and queueing, not shots directly
Cross-provider cost comparison requires estimating runtime first

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why direct shot-based comparison fails

questions.title: Program sets and where the batching discount actually comes from
questions.prompt: Using AWS's own example (100 circuits, 1,000 shots each, on Rigetti Ankaa-3 at $0.30/task + $0.0009/shot), explain exactly where the savings from using a program set come from, and compute the dollar and percentage savings.
questions.modelAnswer: Without program sets: 100*$0.30 + 100,000*$0.0009 = $30.00 + $90.00 = $120.00. With a program set: 1*$0.30 + 100,000*$0.0009 = $0.30 + $90.00 = $90.30. Savings = $29.70, a 24.75% reduction. The per-shot cost is identical in both cases — the entire saving comes from paying the flat per-task fee once instead of 100 times. Batching doesn't reduce the actual quantum work being billed; it eliminates redundant per-task overhead.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be precise that this isn't a 'quantum discount' — it's purely an artifact of the per-task fee structure. If per-shot cost dominated more (e.g., on a pricier device), the percentage saving from batching would shrink accordingly.
commonMistakes: Assuming program sets reduce the per-shot rate itself
Miscounting how many per-task fees are eliminated
Not recognizing the saving scales with the ratio of per-task fee to total per-shot cost, so it varies by device
keyPoints: Without batching: $120.00; with batching: $90.30
Saving comes entirely from eliminating 99 redundant per-task fees
Per-shot cost is unaffected by batching

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct arithmetic for both totals and savings
Correctly attributes the saving to per-task fee elimination

questions.title: Parameter-shift rule cost vs. SPSA's flat per-iteration cost
questions.prompt: Explain why the parameter-shift rule's evaluation cost per iteration scales with parameter count while SPSA's doesn't, and at what point SPSA tends to win on total cost despite needing more iterations to converge.
questions.modelAnswer: Parameter-shift needs 2 evaluations per parameter per iteration (one shifted +, one shifted -) plus 1 for the cost itself: 2p+1 evaluations per iteration. For p=20, that's 41 evaluations/iteration. SPSA perturbs all parameters simultaneously and needs only 2 evaluations per iteration regardless of parameter count. For a 20-parameter circuit at 100 iterations: parameter-shift totals 4,100 evaluations vs. SPSA's 200 — about 20x fewer. SPSA's gradient estimate is noisier, so it typically needs more iterations to reach the same accuracy, but as long as the extra-iterations multiplier stays well below the per-iteration cost ratio (20x here), SPSA still wins on total cost. This crossover is why gradient-free methods dominate in practice once parameter count climbs past a handful.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of it as a ratio problem, not an absolute one: parameter-shift's cost grows linearly with parameters, SPSA's doesn't, so the breakeven point is exactly where SPSA's iteration penalty stops outweighing parameter-shift's per-iteration multiplier.
questions.example: At 1,000 shots/eval on Rigetti Ankaa-3 ($0.30/task+$0.0009/shot): parameter-shift costs $4,920 for 100 iterations vs. SPSA's $240 — even tripling SPSA's iterations to account for noisier convergence ($720) still beats parameter-shift decisively.
commonMistakes: Assuming parameter-shift's exact gradient always wins because it needs fewer iterations
Ignoring that SPSA's extra iterations must be multiplied against its own per-iteration cost, not parameter-shift's
Forgetting the comparison needs an actual iteration-count estimate for SPSA, not just the per-iteration formula
keyPoints: Parameter-shift: 2p+1 evaluations per iteration
SPSA: 2 evaluations per iteration, regardless of parameter count
SPSA wins on total cost once its iteration-count penalty is less than parameter-shift's per-iteration multiplier
Gradient-free methods dominate in practice for circuits with more than a handful of parameters

questions.title: Grover's algorithm iteration count and why it matters before submission
questions.prompt: For an unstructured search over N = 1024 items, compute the expected number of Grover oracle calls, and explain why this number matters before you ever submit a job.
questions.modelAnswer: Grover's search needs approximately (pi/4)*sqrt(N) oracle calls. For N=1024: (pi/4)*sqrt(1024) = (pi/4)*32 ≈ 25.13, so you'd plan for 25 oracle calls. This matters before submission because each oracle call itself has a gate cost — if each call needs, say, 40 two-qubit gates, the full circuit depth before even counting the diffuser is roughly 25*40 = 1,000 two-qubit-gate-equivalents, a number worth checking against the target backend's realistic noise-tolerant depth before paying for a submission that's doomed to drown in noise.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always do this multiplication before touching a backend — it turns 'how many iterations does Grover need' from a textbook fact into an actual feasibility gate I can check against a specific device's coherence budget.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to round to a whole number of iterations
Stopping at the iteration count without translating it into an actual gate-depth estimate
Not checking the resulting depth against the target backend's realistic noise-tolerant depth before submission
keyPoints: Grover iterations ≈ (pi/4)*sqrt(N)
For N=1024, ≈25.13, round to 25
Iteration count must be translated into gate depth for a feasibility check
This should happen before submission, not after a failed run

questions.title: Total shot budget for a full QAOA training run
questions.prompt: A QAOA circuit has p=3 layers (6 variational parameters). Using the parameter-shift rule over 100 optimizer iterations at 2,000 shots per circuit evaluation, compute the total number of circuit executions and the total shot count for the entire run.
questions.modelAnswer: Each parameter needs 2 evaluations under parameter-shift (shifted + and -): evals_per_gradient = 6 params * 2 = 12 circuit executions per gradient step. Over 100 iterations: total_circuit_executions = 12*100 = 1,200. At 2,000 shots per evaluation: total_shots = 1,200*2,000 = 2,400,000. That 2.4 million figure, not 'one circuit at 2,000 shots,' is what actually determines queue cost and runtime — it needs to be calculated before committing to a full training loop on queued real hardware.
questions.professionalAnswer: The number that actually matters is the full-run total, not the per-circuit number — I've seen people quote '2,000 shots' as if that's the job's cost, when the real multiplier from parameters times iterations is 1,200x bigger.
commonMistakes: Reporting shots-per-circuit instead of the total shots across the whole run
Forgetting the gradient-evaluation multiplier (2 evals per parameter) when estimating total executions
Not multiplying through to total shots before estimating cost
keyPoints: 12 circuit executions per gradient step (6 params * 2)
1,200 total circuit executions over 100 iterations
2,400,000 total shots
This total, not the per-circuit shot count, determines real cost and queue burden

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct total executions and total shots
Explains why the full-run total matters

questions.title: Exponential backoff with jitter: computing the delay sequence
questions.prompt: With a base delay of 500ms and a cap of 60,000ms, compute the deterministic exponential backoff cap for attempts 0 through 5, the total worst-case wait, and explain what 'full jitter' adds on top of this.
questions.modelAnswer: attempt 0: min(60000, 500*2^0)=500ms; attempt 1: 1,000ms; attempt 2: 2,000ms; attempt 3: 4,000ms; attempt 4: 8,000ms; attempt 5: 16,000ms. Total worst-case wait across 6 attempts: 31,500ms (~31.5 sec). Full jitter doesn't retry at exactly these delays — it picks a random delay uniformly between 0 and the computed cap for that attempt, which keeps the same overall backoff growth while desynchronizing many clients that hit the same failure simultaneously, preventing a retry storm.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd give the exact sequence first, then immediately explain jitter's purpose isn't to change the growth curve but to stop every client lining up on the same clock tick — that's the part people miss when they implement 'exponential backoff' without jitter.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to cap the delay at the maximum (e.g., computing 500*2^7 without applying the 60,000ms ceiling)
Confusing jitter with randomizing the base delay itself rather than the per-attempt window
Treating backoff and jitter as the same mechanism rather than jitter being layered on top
keyPoints: Delays double each attempt: 500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000ms
Total worst-case wait across 6 attempts: 31,500ms
Full jitter picks a random delay between 0 and the computed cap per attempt
Jitter's purpose is desynchronizing simultaneous retriers, not changing the growth rate

questions.title: Reproducibility, replicability, and robustness — three distinct goals
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between reproducibility, replicability, and robustness in the context of a quantum computing research result, and give an example of a result that could reproduce but fail to replicate.
questions.modelAnswer: Reproducibility: using the original code and data, do you get the same result — testing the original pipeline. Replicability: using a new, independent implementation of the described method on the same or equivalent data, do you get a consistent result — testing the method itself, not one codebase. Robustness: does the result hold under reasonable variations (different seed, comparable device, different problem instance). A result can reproduce (the original script, re-run, gives the original answer) while failing to replicate (an independent implementation of the same described method gives a different answer) — which points to a bug or hidden assumption in the original code, not necessarily a flaw in the underlying idea.
questions.professionalAnswer: I keep these three separate in my head because conflating them leads to the wrong conclusion — a reproduce-but-fail-to-replicate outcome is a code-quality finding about the original paper, not evidence the phenomenon itself is false.
commonMistakes: Using 'reproduce' and 'replicate' interchangeably
Treating a hardware-based reproduction attempt as a pure reproducibility test, ignoring that it's automatically also a robustness check since hardware drifts
Assuming a successful reproduction validates the underlying method rather than just the original pipeline
keyPoints: Reproducibility tests the original pipeline
Replicability tests the method via an independent implementation
Robustness tests sensitivity to reasonable variation
Reproduce-but-fail-to-replicate implicates the original code, not necessarily the idea

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives a coherent example of reproduce-vs-replicate divergence

questions.title: Testable and falsifiable: the two non-negotiable hypothesis properties
questions.prompt: Explain why 'quantum computers are powerful' is not a usable research hypothesis, and what makes a hypothesis both testable and falsifiable, using the GHZ/zero-noise-extrapolation example as a model.
questions.modelAnswer: A hypothesis is testable if some real experiment with measurable outputs could support or contradict it; it's falsifiable if some possible outcome could show it's wrong. 'Quantum computers are powerful' names no measurement and no way to fail — it's neither. 'Zero-noise extrapolation reduces the measured bit-flip error rate of this specific 3-qubit circuit on this specific IBM device, relative to no mitigation, at the 95% confidence level' names the technique, the circuit, the device, the comparison condition, and the direction — it can be run, measured, and could come out false.
questions.professionalAnswer: The test I apply to any proposed hypothesis is simple: can I name an outcome, right now, that would prove this wrong? If I can't, it isn't a hypothesis yet, it's still a research interest.
commonMistakes: Writing a hypothesis with no named comparison condition, making 'improves' unfalsifiable
Confusing an engineering task ('can I implement Grover's in Qiskit') with a hypothesis
Writing a hypothesis whose answer is already certain from known theory, which isn't research
keyPoints: Testable: a real experiment could produce measurable support or contradiction
Falsifiable: some outcome could show the hypothesis is wrong
A named comparison/baseline and a named direction are required
A specific circuit, device, and technique must be named, not 'some hardware'

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses why the vague example fails both properties
Uses the GHZ/ZNE example correctly as a positive model

questions.title: Why quantum SDKs break silently more often than classical libraries
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a 'loud break' and a 'silent break' when upgrading a quantum SDK version, and why pinning exact versions matters more here than for a typical Python library like NumPy.
questions.modelAnswer: A loud break removes an old API, so code raises an immediate AttributeError or ImportError — annoying but safe, since you find out the moment you run anything. A silent break leaves the API in place but changes its numerical behavior, e.g. a transpiler's default optimization behavior changing between versions, producing a different gate decomposition with different depth and noise sensitivity, with no error raised at all. Quantum SDKs like Qiskit have gone through several disruptive version transitions (e.g. the 0.x-to-1.0 removal of qiskit.execute()) as the field matures from exploratory to production-grade, unlike a mature library like NumPy where minor/patch upgrades rarely change behavior. Exact pins (==) plus a committed lockfile are what let a pinned test suite catch a silent break by comparing against previously recorded results — a range pin (>=) can silently resolve to a different version with no warning.
questions.professionalAnswer: The distinction I always make explicit on a team is: loud breaks are a QA problem you'll notice for free; silent breaks are the ones that require you to have already built the safety net — pinned versions plus a regression-tested baseline — before the break happens, not after.
commonMistakes: Assuming any SDK version bump that doesn't throw an error is safe
Using range pins (e.g. qiskit>=1.0) for a quantum SDK the way you would for a stable classical library
Not committing a full lockfile, which still leaves transitive dependencies (rustworkx, symengine) free to resolve differently
keyPoints: Loud break: API removed, errors immediately
Silent break: API still works, numerical output changes with no error
Quantum SDKs churn faster than mature classical libraries
Exact pins + committed lockfile + regression tests catch silent breaks

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes loud vs. silent breaks
Explains why quantum SDKs are riskier than mature classical libraries
Connects pinning/lockfiles to catching silent breaks

questions.title: Coherence time as a feasibility ceiling for circuit depth
questions.prompt: Explain what coherence time is, and why checking a circuit's estimated depth against a backend's coherence time matters before checking anything about shot budget.
questions.modelAnswer: Coherence time is how long qubits maintain their quantum state before decohering into noise. A circuit's depth relative to a backend's coherence time is a feasibility signal: if executing the circuit would take meaningfully longer than the qubits stay coherent, the result will be dominated by noise rather than signal, no matter how many shots you run — more shots make a noisy measurement more precisely noisy, not more correct. This is a feasibility check, distinct from and prior to a cost/precision tradeoff: there's no point optimizing a shot budget for a circuit that's fundamentally infeasible on the target device at any shot count.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat feasibility and cost as two separate gates in that order — qubit count and coherence-time-relative-depth first, because no shot budget fixes an infeasible circuit, then shot budget once feasibility is confirmed.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to shot-budget optimization without first checking depth-vs-coherence feasibility
Assuming more shots can compensate for a circuit that's too deep for the device's coherence time
Checking only qubit count and skipping the depth/coherence check entirely
keyPoints: Coherence time: how long qubits hold state before decohering
Depth vs. coherence time is a feasibility check, not a precision tradeoff
More shots cannot fix a circuit whose depth exceeds the device's noise-tolerant window
Feasibility checks come before shot-budget optimization in a resource-estimation workflow

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why depth/coherence feasibility precedes shot budgeting

questions.title: Global phase vs. a real logic bug in statevector comparison
questions.prompt: Explain why comparing two statevectors with naive equality can produce a false bug report, and what the correct comparison method is.
questions.modelAnswer: Two statevectors that differ only by a global phase (multiplying the entire state by -1 or i, for example) are physically indistinguishable by any possible measurement — no experiment can tell them apart. A naive `assert statevector == expected_statevector` using raw equality will flag them as different anyway, because the underlying complex amplitudes differ even though no observable does. The correct approach is `Statevector.equiv()`, which correctly treats states differing only by global phase as equivalent, avoiding a false-positive 'bug' report for something that isn't actually wrong.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is one of the classic 'looks like a bug, isn't a bug' traps — I always check whether a statevector mismatch is a global-phase difference before spending time debugging gate logic that's actually correct.
commonMistakes: Using raw array/vector equality to compare statevectors instead of a phase-aware comparison
Chasing a 'bug' that's actually just an unmeasurable global phase difference
Not knowing that global phase has zero effect on any measurement outcome
keyPoints: Global phase is unmeasurable and physically irrelevant
Naive equality flags global-phase differences as mismatches incorrectly
Statevector.equiv() correctly ignores global phase
This check belongs early in a debugging order, before suspecting real circuit logic

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains global phase's physical irrelevance
Correctly identifies Statevector.equiv() as the fix

questions.title: Qiskit's bit-ordering convention and why it causes correlation bugs
questions.prompt: Explain Qiskit's default convention for which qubit index corresponds to which position in a reported bitstring, and why mixing this up is one of the most common sources of a 'wrong correlation' bug.
questions.modelAnswer: Qiskit reports bitstrings with qubit 0 as the rightmost bit by default (little-endian relative to qubit index). A bug where you read counts['01'] left-to-right and assume it means 'qubit 0 is 1' when it actually means 'qubit 1 is 1' is extremely common, and it looks exactly like a wrong-correlation bug in a statistical test — a Bell-state test might appear to show the wrong qubits correlated when the circuit logic is actually correct and only the bitstring interpretation is backwards.
questions.professionalAnswer: Any time a correlation pattern looks wrong, I check the bit-ordering interpretation before touching the circuit itself — it's a one-line explanation for a huge fraction of 'the entanglement is backwards' reports.
commonMistakes: Assuming bitstring position left-to-right matches qubit index order
Debugging circuit logic extensively before checking the simpler bit-ordering explanation
Not documenting which convention a codebase uses, causing the same confusion to recur across a team
keyPoints: Qiskit's default: qubit 0 is the rightmost character in a reported bitstring
A reversed interpretation looks identical to a real correlation bug
This should be checked early in a debugging order, before suspecting hardware noise
Documenting the convention prevents repeat confusion across a team

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why it masquerades as a correlation bug

questions.title: Write a statistically-justified measurement assertion helper
questions.prompt: Write a reusable `assert_consistent_with_expected_p(observed_count, n_shots, expected_p, confidence_z)` helper that z-tests a binary measurement outcome, and a test that uses it at the 99% confidence level for a Hadamard circuit.
questions.code:
import math

def z_score_for_binary_outcome(observed_count, n_shots, expected_p):
    phat = observed_count / n_shots
    se = math.sqrt(expected_p * (1 - expected_p) / n_shots)
    return (phat - expected_p) / se

def assert_consistent_with_expected_p(observed_count, n_shots, expected_p, confidence_z=1.96):
    z = z_score_for_binary_outcome(observed_count, n_shots, expected_p)
    assert abs(z) < confidence_z, (
        f"z={z:.3f} exceeds threshold {confidence_z} "
        f"(observed {observed_count}/{n_shots}, expected p={expected_p})"
    )

def test_hadamard_produces_fair_outcomes():
    counts = run_circuit(build_hadamard_circuit(), shots=1024, seed=7)
    assert_consistent_with_expected_p(counts.get('0', 0), 1024, expected_p=0.5, confidence_z=2.58)
questions.modelAnswer: The helper computes phat = observed/n, SE = sqrt(p0(1-p0)/n), and z = (phat-p0)/SE, then asserts |z| is below the chosen confidence_z. The test wires it into a real circuit run with a fixed seed, deliberately using confidence_z=2.58 (99%) rather than the tighter 95% default, with that choice explicit and visible in the test rather than buried as an unstated default. The assertion message includes the actual z-score and the observed/expected values so a failure is immediately diagnosable without re-deriving the arithmetic.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on any version of this helper that hardcodes confidence_z inside the function instead of taking it as a parameter — the whole point of Lesson 5's argument is that the threshold has to be a visible, justified choice at the call site, not a buried default.
commonMistakes: Hardcoding the confidence level inside the helper instead of parameterizing it
Not including the observed/expected values in the assertion failure message
Forgetting to pin a seed on the simulator run, making the test flaky
keyPoints: SE = sqrt(p0(1-p0)/n)
z = (phat - p0)/SE
confidence_z should be an explicit parameter, not a hidden default
Assertion messages should include enough data to diagnose a failure without rerunning

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Confidence level is parameterized and explicit
Code clarity and assertion message quality

questions.title: Write a construction test for a parameterized GHZ circuit
questions.prompt: Write a pytest construction test for `build_ghz_circuit(n_qubits)` that verifies qubit count, exact gate sequence, and that every CX gate uses qubit 0 as the control — without ever executing the circuit.
questions.modelAnswer: The test inspects `qc.data`, a list of CircuitInstruction objects, without running the circuit at all. It asserts num_qubits matches the input, that the gate name sequence is exactly ['h','cx','cx','cx'] for n=4 (catching an off-by-one or a missing Hadamard), and that every CX's control qubit index is 0 (catching a swapped-qubit bug). This runs in milliseconds with no simulator or backend dependency, which is exactly why construction tests should make up the majority of a quantum test suite and run on every commit.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd emphasize in review that this test catches real bugs — an off-by-one in the loop range or a transposed control/target — with zero flakiness and zero backend cost, which is why it belongs in the fast CI tier, not the nightly statistical-test tier.
commonMistakes: Running the circuit on a simulator just to check its structure, when `circuit.data` already exposes it
Checking gate count but not which qubits each gate acts on
Not parametrizing the test across multiple qubit counts to catch size-specific off-by-ones

Construction tests are fast, deterministic, and backend-free
Checking control-qubit index catches swapped-qubit bugs specifically
These tests should run on every commit, not just nightly

Covers gate sequence and control-qubit assertions
Explains why this belongs in the fast CI tier

questions.title: Parametrize a construction test across multiple circuit sizes
questions.prompt: Using pytest.mark.parametrize, write one test function that verifies build_ghz_circuit(n_qubits) produces exactly n_qubits-1 CX gates, for n_qubits in [2, 3, 5, 8].
questions.code:
import pytest

@pytest.mark.parametrize("n_qubits", [2, 3, 5, 8])
def test_ghz_circuit_structure_across_sizes(n_qubits):
    qc = build_ghz_circuit(n_qubits)
    assert qc.num_qubits == n_qubits
    cx_count = sum(1 for instr in qc.data if instr.operation.name == "cx")
    assert cx_count == n_qubits - 1
questions.modelAnswer: pytest.mark.parametrize runs the same test body once per value in the list, reporting each as a separate test case. This matters specifically for construction tests because an off-by-one bug (e.g. `range(1, n_qubits - 1)` instead of `range(1, n_qubits)`) might only manifest at certain sizes — testing only n=4 could miss a bug that only shows up at n=2 or n=8, so covering a spread of sizes in one maintainable test function is deliberately more robust than one hardcoded case.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd flag any PR that tests a circuit-building function at only one hardcoded size as under-tested — parametrize costs almost nothing to add and catches size-dependent off-by-ones that a single case simply can't.
commonMistakes: Testing only one hardcoded qubit count, missing size-dependent bugs
Duplicating the test body manually for each size instead of using parametrize
Not asserting num_qubits alongside gate count, missing a different class of bug
keyPoints: pytest.mark.parametrize avoids duplicated test code across input sizes
Off-by-one bugs can be size-specific, so testing only one size is insufficient
Each parametrized case is reported separately on failure

questions.title: Write a statevector exactness test for a Bell pair
questions.prompt: Write a test using Qiskit's Statevector simulator that verifies a Bell-pair circuit produces exactly {'00': 0.5, '11': 0.5} with no sampling noise, and explain why this test needs no shot count.
questions.code:
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector

def test_bell_pair_statevector_is_exact():
    qc = build_bell_pair()
    sv = Statevector.from_instruction(qc)
    probabilities = sv.probabilities_dict()
    assert set(probabilities.keys()) == {'00', '11'}
    assert abs(probabilities['00'] - 0.5) < 1e-9
    assert abs(probabilities['11'] - 0.5) < 1e-9
questions.modelAnswer: Statevector.from_instruction returns exact amplitudes rather than sampled counts, so there is no sampling noise in the picture at all — probabilities come out as exact mathematical values (0.5 and 0.5, tested against a tight 1e-9 tolerance for floating point, not a statistical tolerance). This is a ground-truth logic check: if it fails, the bug is in the circuit's construction logic itself, with no 'maybe it's just noise' excuse available, since a statevector simulator has none. If this passes but a shot-based statistical test still fails, the bug lives elsewhere — tolerance setting or real backend noise.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat a statevector test as the fastest way to rule out 'is this a real logic bug' before spending any time on shot-based statistical testing — it removes sampling noise from the question entirely.
commonMistakes: Using a statistical tolerance (like a z-score threshold) instead of a tight floating-point tolerance for an exact statevector check
Running this against a noisy simulator or real hardware, which reintroduces the noise this test is designed to eliminate
Skipping this check and going straight to shot-based statistical testing, losing the ability to cleanly isolate a logic bug
keyPoints: Statevector simulation has zero sampling noise
Use a tight floating-point tolerance (e.g. 1e-9), not a statistical threshold
A failure here means the bug is in circuit logic, not noise
This should run before, and separately from, shot-based statistical tests

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct use of Statevector.from_instruction and probabilities_dict
Explains why no shot count or statistical threshold is needed

Adding hardware-only methods (like get_queue_position) to the shared interface
Not including name() for logging/reproducibility records

Algorithm code depends only on the interface, never a concrete backend

questions.title: Normalize a classical feature vector for amplitude encoding
questions.prompt: Write code that normalizes the classical vector [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6] for amplitude encoding, verifies the normalized vector's squared entries sum to 1, and states how many qubits it requires.
questions.code:
import math

raw = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]
sum_sq = sum(x**2 for x in raw)
norm = math.sqrt(sum_sq)
normalized = [x / norm for x in raw]
check = sum(x**2 for x in normalized)
n_qubits = math.log2(len(raw))

assert abs(check - 1.0) < 1e-9
print(normalized, n_qubits)
questions.modelAnswer: sum of squares = 3^2+1^2+4^2+1^2+5^2+9^2+2^2+6^2 = 173; norm = sqrt(173) ≈ 13.1529. normalized = raw/norm ≈ [0.2281, 0.0760, 0.3041, 0.0760, 0.3801, 0.6843, 0.1521, 0.4562]. The normalized vector's squared entries sum to exactly 1.0 by construction, satisfying the quantum state's unit-norm constraint. With 8 features, log2(8) = 3 qubits are needed to index them for amplitude encoding. This normalization is 100% classical computation — nothing about it happens on a QPU — and must happen before the vector is ever loaded as circuit amplitudes, since skipping it either fails validation or silently rescales the data in an unintended way.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd flag any amplitude-encoding pipeline that loads a feature vector into a circuit without an explicit, tested normalization step upstream — that's a classical bug waiting to produce a confidently wrong answer, not a quantum one.
commonMistakes: Dividing by the sum of squares instead of its square root (the norm)
Forgetting the unit-norm check as an explicit assertion in the pipeline
Using angle encoding's qubit-per-feature count instead of log2(n) for amplitude encoding
keyPoints: Normalize by dividing by sqrt(sum of squares)
Normalized vector's squared entries must sum to exactly 1
Amplitude encoding needs log2(n) qubits for n features
Normalization is mandatory classical preprocessing, not optional

from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
import json

class ExperimentRecord:
    git_commit: str
    experiment_tag: str
    sdk_name: str
    sdk_version: str
    backend_name: str
    seed_simulator: int | None
    seed_transpiler: int | None
    shots: int
    timestamp_utc: str

Hand-typing the metadata file instead of generating it programmatically from the actual run
Not tying the record's experiment_tag to the git tag used for the code
keyPoints: Record must capture seed_simulator, seed_transpiler, and shots separately
SDK version must be recorded alongside any seed
Generate the record programmatically, not by hand
Commit it alongside the tagged commit for full traceability

questions.title: Implement exponential backoff with full jitter for a retry loop
questions.prompt: Write a function `backoff_delay_ms(attempt, base_ms=500, cap_ms=60000)` that returns the deterministic cap for a given attempt, plus a `jittered_delay_ms(attempt, ...)` that returns a randomized full-jitter delay.
questions.modelAnswer: backoff_delay_ms computes min(cap_ms, base_ms * 2^attempt), giving the sequence 500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000ms for attempts 0 through 5 (total worst-case 31,500ms across 6 attempts). jittered_delay_ms doesn't wait exactly that cap — it picks a uniformly random delay between 0 and the cap for that attempt, which keeps the overall backoff growth while desynchronizing simultaneous retriers, directly preventing the retry-storm effect that fixed-interval or non-jittered exponential retry causes under provider-side congestion.
questions.professionalAnswer: The review flag I'd raise on this code is whether jitter is applied per-attempt against that attempt's own cap, not against a single global cap — getting that wrong defeats the desynchronization jitter is meant to provide.
commonMistakes: Not capping the exponential growth, letting delay grow unbounded for high attempt counts
Applying jitter as a fixed random offset added to the cap instead of a uniform draw between 0 and the cap
Forgetting to combine this with a max-attempt or cumulative-time stopping rule
keyPoints: Deterministic cap: min(cap_ms, base_ms * 2^attempt)
Full jitter: uniform random delay between 0 and that attempt's cap
Jitter desynchronizes simultaneous retriers without changing overall growth
Needs a separate stopping rule (max attempts or cumulative time budget)

questions.title: Implement a cost ceiling circuit-breaker inside an optimization loop
questions.prompt: Write pseudocode/Python for a VQE-style loop that tracks cumulative spend as it runs and halts with an alert if spend crosses a pre-set ceiling, independent of the max-iteration cap.
questions.code:
COST_CEILING_USD = 500.00
cumulative_spend = 0.0

for iteration in range(max_iterations):
    circuit = build_circuit(params)
    counts = backend.run(circuit, shots=shots)
    cumulative_spend += estimate_cost(per_task_fee, per_shot_fee, shots)

Relying solely on a max-iteration cap, assuming the loop will converge before becoming expensive
Not alerting a human when the ceiling is hit, silently stopping with no visibility

The cost ceiling check is independent of the iteration-count cap

questions.title: Instrument a VQE loop to split classical time from quantum time
questions.prompt: Write a `ProfileAccumulator` dataclass and instrumented `run_vqe_iteration` function that separately tracks classical_time and quantum_time across many iterations.
questions.code:
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class ProfileAccumulator:
    classical_time: float = 0.0
    quantum_time: float = 0.0
    n_iterations: int = 0

def run_vqe_iteration(params, backend, acc: ProfileAccumulator):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    circuit = bind_ansatz_parameters(params)
    t1 = time.perf_counter()
    counts = backend.run(circuit, shots=1024)
    t2 = time.perf_counter()
    expectation = compute_expectation_from_counts(counts)
    t3 = time.perf_counter()
    acc.classical_time += (t1 - t0) + (t3 - t2)
    acc.quantum_time += (t2 - t1)
    acc.n_iterations += 1
    return expectation
questions.modelAnswer: Four timestamps bracket the two classical steps (binding parameters, computing the expectation value) and the one quantum step (backend.run). classical_time accumulates the two classical intervals; quantum_time accumulates only the backend.run interval. This split answers the question that matters — what fraction of total wall-clock time is actually the quantum part versus ordinary Python work — which a single undifferentiated 'total time' number cannot answer, and which determines whether cProfile (for classical code) or queue-wait analysis (for real hardware) is the right next tool.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ask whoever profiles a hybrid loop to show me this split before any optimization discussion — without it, people instinctively start optimizing the classical code even when queue wait on real hardware is 97% of the actual time.
commonMistakes: Measuring only total wall-clock time per iteration without separating classical and quantum portions
Applying cProfile directly to a real-hardware backend.run() call expecting useful output
Not accumulating across many iterations, making the split too noisy to act on
keyPoints: Classical time: parameter binding + expectation computation
Quantum time: backend.run() only
This split determines which profiling tool is useful next
On real hardware, a third category (queue wait) should be split out separately

Explains why this split matters for next steps

# Step 1: inspect construction, no execution needed
for instr in qc.data:
    print(instr.operation.name, [q._index for q in instr.qubits])
# Suppose output shows: h [0], cx [1, 0]  <- control=1, target=0, but intended cx(0, 1)

# Step 2: confirm with statevector (no sampling noise)

Running on real hardware to debug, re-introducing noise that obscures a pure logic bug
Fixing the symptom (re-running with more shots) instead of the actual swapped-qubit cause

questions.title: Write a deterministic transpilation depth-budget test
questions.prompt: Write a test that transpiles a Bell circuit against a fake backend with a fixed transpiler seed and asserts the resulting depth is within a budget, explaining why the seed must be pinned.
questions.code:
from qiskit import transpile
from qiskit.providers.fake_provider import FakeManilaV2

def test_bell_circuit_transpiles_within_depth_budget():
    qc = build_bell_pair()
    backend = FakeManilaV2()
    transpiled = transpile(qc, backend=backend, optimization_level=1, seed_transpiler=42)
    assert transpiled.depth() <= 6
    assert transpiled.num_qubits == backend.num_qubits
questions.modelAnswer: seed_transpiler=42 is pinned because at optimization_level 1+, Qiskit's transpiler can use randomized heuristics for qubit layout and routing — without a fixed seed, the exact same logical circuit can transpile to a different depth between otherwise-identical runs, making the depth assertion flaky rather than deterministic. Pinning the seed makes the output depth and gate count deterministic for this specific circuit, backend, and optimization level, so the test reliably catches a real depth regression instead of occasionally failing on random layout variance.

Asserting an exact depth instead of a budget (<=), making the test brittle to minor transpiler version changes
Not also checking num_qubits matches the backend, missing a different feasibility issue

seed_transpiler pins that randomness for deterministic, reproducible test output

questions.title: A generic retry handler blindly resubmits a circuit-validation failure
questions.prompt: A job fails with a circuit validation error on its first attempt (the circuit violates a device constraint). Your orchestration code's generic retry handler automatically resubmits it three times before giving up. What's wrong with this behavior, and what should the code do instead?
questions.modelAnswer: A circuit validation failure is a classical bug in the submission code — the circuit itself violates a device constraint (too many qubits, an unsupported gate, exceeding max depth) and is rejected before ever queueing. Resubmitting the identical invalid circuit will fail identically every single time; this failure mode is explicitly not retryable, unlike a queue timeout or transient network error. The orchestration code should classify the failure by type first (using a decision table: queue timeout → retry, device offline → retry on a different device, transient network error → retry, circuit validation failure → do not retry), and for a validation failure, surface the specific constraint violation immediately so it can be fixed in code, rather than wasting three attempts and the associated latency/API overhead on something that cannot succeed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd call this out directly in a post-incident review: one generic try/except/retry block treating every failure the same is the root cause here, not the validation error itself — the fix is a failure-mode-aware dispatcher, not a smarter retry count.
commonMistakes: Treating every failure type with the same generic retry logic
Not surfacing the specific validation error message, making the real bug harder to find
Wasting retry budget and latency on a failure mode that can never succeed on resubmission
keyPoints: Circuit validation failures are not retryable — they're a code bug
A decision table should classify failures before deciding retry vs. fallback
Retrying an identical invalid circuit always fails identically
The fix is error-mode-aware dispatch, not a one-size-fits-all retry block

questions.title: Debugging order when a statistical test fails
questions.prompt: A statistical test for a circuit's measurement outcomes fails. Walk through the correct order of causes to investigate, cheapest and most likely first, and explain why jumping straight to 'hardware noise' is usually the wrong first move.
questions.modelAnswer: The correct order: (1) re-run construction tests — a huge fraction of 'wrong result' bugs are a swapped qubit index, a gate on the wrong qubit, or an off-by-one, all things a construction test should catch; (2) run a noiseless statevector simulator to check the circuit's exact logic with zero sampling noise, isolating whether the bug is in the circuit's logic at all; (3) re-check whether the statistical test's tolerance was set appropriately for the shot count used, since an overly tight tolerance produces false failures on correct code; (4) only after ruling out 1-3, consider real hardware noise, confirmed by comparing the noiseless-simulator result against the noisy-simulator or hardware result. Jumping straight to 'hardware noise' skips three cheaper, more common explanations and can waste hours chasing a phenomenon that isn't actually present.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat this order as non-negotiable in code review — 'maybe it's just noisy hardware' is the single most common excuse for not actually debugging, and it's almost never the first explanation that should be checked.
commonMistakes: Suspecting hardware noise before checking construction and statevector logic
Skipping the statevector check, which would cleanly rule logic bugs in or out with zero sampling noise
Not re-checking whether the test's tolerance was appropriate for the shot count before blaming the circuit or the hardware
keyPoints: Order: construction tests → statevector check → tolerance check → hardware/noise
Statevector simulation has zero sampling noise, cleanly isolating logic bugs
An overly tight tolerance can produce false failures on correct code
Hardware noise should be the last, not first, suspect

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why each step is cheaper/more likely than the next

questions.title: A VQE loop runs for three hours with no convergence and no cost alert
questions.prompt: Your team's VQE loop has been running for three hours with no convergence and no cost alert triggered. Using the common hybrid architecture mistakes you know, diagnose which mistakes likely contributed and the specific fix for each.
questions.modelAnswer: Three likely contributing mistakes: (1) No cost ceiling/circuit-breaker on the loop — optimizers sometimes oscillate, plateau without triggering their own tolerance check, or diverge from a bug, and without tracking cumulative spend inside the loop itself (not just in a billing dashboard after the fact), nobody notices until hours of real-hardware spend have accumulated. Fix: add an in-loop cumulative-spend check against a pre-set ceiling, independent of the iteration cap. (2) Possibly developing/debugging directly against real hardware instead of a simulator — if this is still a debugging run rather than a final validation run, it should be on a free/near-free simulator. Fix: move iterative debugging to a classical simulator, reserve hardware for confirmatory runs. (3) Ignoring shot noise when judging convergence — if the convergence check compares cost values without accounting for standard error, the optimizer may never register as 'improved' due to noise, appearing to not converge when it actually has within statistical uncertainty. Fix: set convergence tolerance relative to the expected shot-noise floor, not an arbitrarily tight number.
questions.professionalAnswer: In an actual incident review I'd want the cumulative-spend log pulled first — that single number tells you immediately whether this is a cost-ceiling miss, and from there whether it's a hardware-vs-simulator mistake or a tolerance-vs-noise mistake becomes easy to distinguish.
commonMistakes: Assuming the loop will 'eventually converge' without a hard cost ceiling
Debugging a not-yet-verified loop directly against paid real hardware
Setting convergence tolerance without accounting for the shot-noise floor
keyPoints: Missing cost ceiling lets spend run unchecked regardless of convergence
Real hardware is the wrong place to debug an unverified loop
Convergence tolerance must account for shot noise, not be arbitrarily tight
Each mistake has a specific, named fix, not a vague 'be more careful'

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the cost-ceiling mistake and fix
Correctly identifies the simulator-vs-hardware mistake and fix
Correctly identifies the shot-noise/tolerance mistake and fix

questions.title: cProfile reports backend.run() as the bottleneck on real hardware
questions.prompt: A teammate runs cProfile on their entire VQE script, including the real-hardware backend.run() calls, and concludes 'the bottleneck is backend.run(), so I need to optimize my code's call to it.' What's wrong with that conclusion, and what should they profile instead?
questions.modelAnswer: cProfile is a deterministic Python profiler useful for CPU-bound classical code, but applying it to a network/queue-bound call like backend.run() against real hardware just faithfully reports that most time was spent 'waiting' — it tells you nothing actionable, because the time isn't being spent executing your code at all. On real hardware, queue wait regularly dominates total wall-clock time by orders of magnitude (one profiled example showed 97% queue wait, 2% classical, 1% device execution) and has nothing to do with code efficiency. They should instead instrument the pipeline to separately track queue_wait_time (job_started_executing_at - job_submitted_at) and device_execution_time (job_completed_at - job_started_executing_at) as distinct categories from classical time, and apply cProfile only to the genuinely CPU-bound classical portions once the split confirms that's actually where time is going.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd redirect the conversation immediately: cProfile answering 'backend.run() is slow' on real hardware is a true but useless statement — the actionable question is how much of that was queue wait versus actual device time, and that needs separate instrumentation, not a CPU profiler.
commonMistakes: Applying a CPU profiler to a network/queue-bound call and treating its output as actionable
Trying to 'optimize' a call to backend.run() when the delay is queue wait, not code inefficiency
Not separating queue wait from device execution time as distinct categories
keyPoints: cProfile is only informative for CPU-bound classical code
Queue wait on real hardware can dominate total time by orders of magnitude
The fix is instrumenting queue_wait_time and device_execution_time separately
No amount of code optimization reduces queue wait

questions.title: SDK upgrade: no import errors, but a statistical test now fails by a wide margin
questions.prompt: Your team upgrades from qiskit==1.1.0 to qiskit==1.2.4. No import errors occur, but a statistical test that previously passed now fails by a wide margin. Walk through which two things from a safe-upgrade checklist you'd check first, and why a 'loud break' assumption would have missed this.
questions.modelAnswer: A 'loud break' assumption (no errors = safe) misses silent breaks entirely — the API still runs, but its numerical behavior changed, which is exactly what produces a statistical-test failure with zero import errors. The two things to check first: (1) whether any transpiler optimization-level default or default random seed/backend configuration changed between 1.1.0 and 1.2.4, since these are the most common sources of silent breaks and directly affect circuit structure and noise sensitivity; (2) re-run the unit/construction tests from the pinned environment against the new version and compare against previously recorded, pinned-environment results, to isolate whether the break is in circuit construction (caught early, cheaply) versus a deeper numerical change in the statistical layer. Only after these checks would you escalate to reading the full changelog line-by-line for every version crossed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The instinct I correct here every time is 'no errors means it's fine' — for quantum SDKs specifically, that's backwards; the dangerous case is exactly the one with no errors, because nothing forces you to notice until a downstream test like this one catches it.
commonMistakes: Assuming an upgrade is safe because no import or runtime errors occurred
Not checking whether default transpiler/seed/backend configuration changed between versions
Jumping to blaming the hardware or 'random bad luck' instead of the version bump itself
keyPoints: Silent breaks produce no errors but change numerical output
Transpiler default and seed/config changes are the most common silent-break source
Comparing against previously recorded pinned-environment results isolates the cause
'No errors' is not evidence of safety for a quantum SDK upgrade

questions.title: A result record is missing seed_transpiler and a re-run doesn't match
questions.prompt: A result record captures seed_simulator=42 and shots=1024 but not seed_transpiler. A later re-run with the recorded seed and shots still produces a visibly different fidelity number. Explain the most likely reason.
questions.modelAnswer: seed_transpiler controls randomized heuristics the transpiler may use for qubit layout and routing, which is a distinct source of randomness from seed_simulator (which only controls sampling of measurement outcomes from the underlying probability distribution). Without a recorded seed_transpiler, the re-run can transpile the identical logical circuit into a structurally different circuit — different gate decomposition, different depth — which then produces a genuinely different fidelity result even with the simulator seed held fixed, because the thing that actually ran differs. The fix is recording seed_transpiler alongside seed_simulator in every experiment record; a record capturing only one of the two randomness layers is only partially reproducible.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the exact trap the lesson on recording seeds warns about — 'I recorded a seed' sounds complete, but there can be more than one layer of randomness in a pipeline, and missing even one makes the whole record non-reproducible.
commonMistakes: Assuming one recorded seed covers all sources of randomness in the pipeline
Not distinguishing seed_simulator (sampling) from seed_transpiler (layout/routing)
Treating the re-run discrepancy as hardware drift when it's actually a missing transpiler seed on what might even be a pure simulator run
keyPoints: seed_simulator controls sampling; seed_transpiler controls layout/routing heuristics
These are independent sources of randomness
A missing seed_transpiler means the actual executed circuit structure can differ between runs
A complete experiment record needs both seeds, not just one

questions.title: A job fails twice before succeeding — diagnosing wasted spend
questions.prompt: A job fails twice (device-offline, then partial-shot-completion) before succeeding on its third attempt, on IonQ Aria ($0.30/task + $0.03/shot, 1,000 shots/task). Compute the wasted spend from the two failed attempts and explain why an orchestration layer with no error handling makes this worse, not just equally bad.
questions.modelAnswer: Wasted spend = 2 * ($0.30 + 1,000*$0.03) = 2 * $30.30 = $60.60. This is money spent on failure modes that reached the device but produced no usable result, as opposed to a pre-queue validation failure which costs nothing. An orchestration layer with no error handling doesn't just fail cleanly at this point — if it retries blindly in a loop with no circuit-breaker (Chapter 1's Mistake 3), it can keep incurring this $30.30-per-attempt cost indefinitely with zero visibility into cumulative waste, turning a two-failure, $60.60 incident into a potentially unbounded one.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd always separate 'what did this specific incident cost' from 'what could an unguarded retry loop have cost' — $60.60 is the bounded answer here only because this orchestration apparently did stop after three attempts; without a circuit breaker, that bound doesn't exist.
commonMistakes: Assuming failed jobs cost nothing because they didn't produce a usable result
Not distinguishing billed failures (reached the device) from free failures (rejected pre-queue)
Missing that an ungoverned retry loop turns a bounded cost into an unbounded one
keyPoints: Wasted spend: 2 * $30.30 = $60.60
Failures that reach the device (offline, partial completion) still bill
Failures caught before queueing (validation) cost nothing
A missing circuit breaker turns a bounded incident into an unbounded one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes billed vs. unbilled failure types

questions.title: Fixed-interval retry makes congestion worse during a provider outage
questions.prompt: During a period of provider-side congestion, every client retrying failed jobs on a fixed 1-second interval seems to make the congestion worse, not better. Diagnose why, and name the specific fix.
questions.modelAnswer: Fixed-interval retrying creates synchronized retry storms: when many clients hit the same congestion-caused failure near-simultaneously and all retry after exactly the same delay, their retries also land near-simultaneously, adding another synchronized burst of load to an already-congested system — worsening exactly the condition that caused the original failures. The fix is exponential backoff with jitter: each retry waits longer than the last (a doubling pattern) with randomization added so that even many clients failing at the same moment don't retry in lockstep. This is a standard distributed-systems fix, not something specific to quantum workloads, directly applicable here because cloud quantum providers have the same queue/congestion dynamics as any shared remote service.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd name this immediately as a retry storm and point at the fix by name — exponential backoff with full jitter — because this is a well-understood distributed-systems failure pattern, and quantum cloud providers are not a special case that needs a different solution.
commonMistakes: Treating this as a provider-side problem only, missing the client-side fixed-interval retry as the amplifying cause
Adding exponential backoff without jitter, which still allows some synchronization
Not recognizing this as the same pattern seen in any distributed system under load, requiring a standard fix
keyPoints: Fixed-interval retry synchronizes many clients' retries, worsening congestion
This is called a retry storm
The fix is exponential backoff with jitter
Jitter specifically desynchronizes simultaneous retriers

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly names exponential backoff with jitter as the fix

questions.title: A six-month-old result can no longer be exactly reproduced
questions.prompt: A colleague asks you to re-verify a fidelity number reported six months ago. The pinned SDK version from that run can no longer be installed (the package index removed the release). What should you do, and what should you explicitly avoid doing?
questions.modelAnswer: First, document explicitly that exact reproduction under the original pinned version is no longer possible, rather than silently re-running on a different version and reporting the same old number as if nothing changed. Then re-run the experiment under the closest currently-installable version and report the new result as a new, separately tagged experiment, not a patch overwriting the old one. If the new and old numbers disagree, that discrepancy is itself worth investigating and documenting — it may reveal a silent break between SDK versions — rather than quietly discarding whichever number is less convenient. The git tag plus lockfile approach, if it was followed at the time, lets you retrieve the exact original environment specification even if it can no longer be installed, which is itself useful documentation of what changed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The failure mode I watch for here is quietly re-running on a newer version and reporting the old number unchanged, as if the re-verification confirmed something it didn't — the honest move is a new tagged result plus an explicit note about what couldn't be reproduced exactly.

Discarding a discrepancy between old and new results instead of investigating and documenting it

questions.title: A teammate wants to add get_queue_position() to the shared backend interface
questions.prompt: A teammate wants to add get_queue_position() to the shared QuantumBackend interface so 'all backends have it.' Explain why this is a problem, and where get_queue_position() should actually live.
questions.modelAnswer: This is capability leakage: real hardware exposes things a simulator fundamentally cannot — queue position, calibration data, qubit-specific error rates. Forcing get_queue_position() into the shared QuantumBackend interface means a simulator backend would have to fake a meaningless return value just to satisfy the contract, polluting the common interface every backend must implement. Instead, hardware-specific capabilities should live behind a separate, optional interface (or a hardware-specific subclass) that algorithm code only reaches for when it explicitly knows it's targeting real hardware, keeping the shared contract (run(), name()) clean for every backend.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on this in design review with the simulator test: if implementing this method honestly for every backend type is impossible without faking a value, it doesn't belong in the shared interface — full stop.

Faking a meaningless return value in a simulator backend just to satisfy an interface contract
Not recognizing this pattern as a named mistake (capability leakage) with a known fix

questions.title: An unexpected capstone result contradicts the stated hypothesis
questions.prompt: Your capstone hypothesis predicted the 5-qubit mitigation improvement would be smaller than the 3-qubit one. The actual data shows the 5-qubit reduction (0.160) is slightly larger than the 3-qubit reduction (0.155). Diagnose this using a discrepancy checklist, and state what you'd do next.
questions.modelAnswer: First check implementation bugs in the 5-qubit circuit/noise-scaling code — if clean, check parameter mismatches (shot counts, noise-scaling factors identical across both conditions) — if clean, check whether the two conditions actually ran under comparable device states: were the 3- and 5-qubit jobs genuinely interleaved, or did a queue delay put them hours apart across a recalibration window? If the run log shows a multi-hour gap spanning a recalibration, the most likely explanation isn't that the underlying mechanism is wrong — it's that the two conditions weren't run under comparable device states, exactly the confound interleaving exists to prevent. This is a design/execution limitation, not necessarily a falsified hypothesis. Next steps: if time allows, re-run both conditions genuinely interleaved within one calibration window for a cleaner test; if not, report the result exactly as measured, name the calibration-window gap explicitly as the likely confound in the limitations section, and do not quietly rewrite the hypothesis to match the data (HARKing).
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk the checklist in order out loud, because the tempting move here is to treat 'the data surprised me' as either a bug to hide or a discovery to overclaim — the actual discipline is checking the boring explanations (implementation, parameters, calibration timing) before concluding anything interesting.
commonMistakes: Immediately assuming the hypothesis's underlying mechanism is wrong without checking confounds first
Quietly rewriting the hypothesis after seeing the data to match the outcome (HARKing)
Not checking whether the two conditions were run in the same calibration window

A calibration-window gap between conditions is a classic confound, not a falsified hypothesis

questions.title: Your reproduction doesn't match the paper — diagnosing the gap
questions.prompt: You reproduce a GHZ/zero-noise-extrapolation example and measure a smaller error reduction than the paper reports. Your circuit matches your methodology document, and your shot count and scaling factors match. Walk through the next diagnostic steps and a plausible conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer: With implementation (circuit matches methodology) and parameters (shots, scaling factors match) both ruled out, the next step is checking specification gaps you may have had to fill in yourself — revisit the paper's appendix for a detail you might have missed on first read. A realistic finding: you used linear extrapolation instead of the paper's specified Richardson extrapolation, a gap you hadn't flagged because you missed that detail in the appendix. Re-running with Richardson extrapolation closes most of the gap. The honest conclusion is that the discrepancy was caused by an extraction error on your part — a methodology detail missed on first read — not a flaw in the paper's claim. This is a normal, useful, and honestly reportable outcome, not a failure.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd specifically check the paper's appendix again before considering anything more exotic — extraction gaps hiding in an appendix are a far more common explanation than a genuine flaw in the paper, and this lesson's whole point is ruling out your own gaps before escalating the claim.

questions.title: A device-offline failure during a queued job — retry on same or different device?
questions.prompt: A job queued on a specific device fails because the device went offline for recalibration mid-queue. Should your orchestration code simply retry on the same device? Explain the correct handling.
questions.modelAnswer: No — retrying on the same offline device wastes time, since it will fail again until recalibration finishes, with no predictable timeline. The correct handling, per the retryable-failure decision table, is 'yes, but fall over to an alternate device' — retry the job on a different available device rather than waiting on the same one. This is listed as the first-preference fallback option generally: retry on a different, available device, which handles the device-offline case directly, often at only a small cost/latency penalty compared to waiting indefinitely for the original device.
questions.professionalAnswer: The distinction I'd make explicit is 'retryable' vs. 'retryable on the same resource' — device-offline is retryable, but only if the retry target changes; retrying identically just queues you behind the same outage.

questions.title: No lockfile was committed — what's missing for reproduction?
questions.prompt: A reported result's git tag exists, but no lockfile was ever committed alongside it — only a pyproject.toml with qiskit>=1.0 (a range, not an exact pin). Explain concretely what's now missing to reproduce the result, even though the exact code commit is retrievable.
questions.modelAnswer: The exact code is retrievable via the git tag, but a range pin (qiskit>=1.0) with no lockfile means the actual resolved environment at the time — which specific qiskit version, and critically which versions of its transitive dependencies (rustworkx, symengine, etc.) — was never captured. Re-installing from qiskit>=1.0 today would likely resolve to a newer version than was actually used, and since quantum SDKs have frequent silent breaking changes, a different resolved version can change numerical behavior (a different transpiler default, a different internal random-number generator behavior) without any error. Without the lockfile, there is no way to know which exact environment produced the original result, so 'the code' alone — even with the exact commit retrievable — is not enough to reproduce it.

questions.title: A capstone's exciting mismatch turns out to be a bug, not a discovery

questions.title: Partial shot completion returns fewer shots than requested
questions.prompt: A real-hardware job completes only 600 of the requested 1,000 shots before a transient hardware fault partway through, returning a counts dictionary with the reduced total. How should your orchestration code decide whether to use this result or retry?
questions.modelAnswer: Per the retryability decision table, partial shot completion is a 'depends' case: if the 600 completed shots are enough to meet the use case's required standard error (computed via SE = sqrt(p(1-p)/n)), the result can be treated as a usable partial result; otherwise it should be retried (ideally for the remaining shots or the full job, depending on whether partial-result aggregation is supported). The orchestration code should never silently treat a 600-shot result as if it were the requested 1,000-shot result without first checking whether 600 shots clears the precision bar the downstream decision actually needs — doing otherwise is exactly the kind of degraded-iteration risk that should be explicitly flagged, not silently absorbed into the optimizer.
questions.professionalAnswer: The question I'd ask first is 'does 600 shots meet the precision this decision needs,' not 'is 600 close enough to 1,000' — those are different questions, and only the first one is actually relevant.
commonMistakes: Treating any completed-but-short result as automatically good enough
Silently feeding a degraded (under-shot) result into an optimizer without flagging it
Not computing whether the actual completed shot count meets the use case's precision requirement

questions.title: Designing a backend-abstraction interface that doesn't leak hardware capabilities
questions.prompt: You're architecting the backend layer for a new hybrid quantum project that must run against both a local simulator and real IBM hardware. Design the shared interface: what belongs in it, what doesn't, and why.
questions.modelAnswer: Define an abstract QuantumBackend with exactly two methods every implementation can honestly support: run(circuit, shots) -> counts, and name() -> str for logging/reproducibility. Those belong behind a separate, optional interface or hardware-specific subclass that algorithm code reaches for only when it explicitly knows it's targeting real hardware.

questions.title: Deciding whether a multi-SDK adapter layer is worth building
questions.prompt: A product manager asks you to add Q# support to a Qiskit-only codebase 'in case we need it later.' Using the SDK-adapter pattern, explain what you'd actually recommend and why.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd recommend against building the adapter layer speculatively. The SDK-adapter pattern (an abstract SDKAdapter returning a shared NeutralResult, with Qiskit running in-process and Q# isolated via subprocess into a separate environment) adds real, ongoing overhead — process boundaries, a neutral result format, two environments to maintain. It's worth that cost when there's a genuine, current need: comparing hardware vendors, validating a result independent of any one SDK's bugs, or supporting customers standardized on different toolchains. 'In case we need it later' is exactly the speculative-abstraction trap this pattern warns against — the fix is adding the adapter layer when a second SDK becomes an actual current requirement, not before, consistent with not over-engineering the single-SDK backend interface either.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame the pushback in terms of carrying cost, not principle: every month this adapter layer exists without a real second-SDK need, we're maintaining two environments and an abstraction for a requirement that doesn't exist yet — that's a cost with no current payoff.
commonMistakes: Building speculative architecture for a hypothetical future requirement
Underestimating the ongoing maintenance cost of two isolated SDK environments
Not naming the specific, concrete trigger (a real second-SDK need) that would justify building it
keyPoints: SDK-adapter pattern adds real, ongoing complexity
Worth it only for a genuine current need (vendor comparison, cross-validation, customer requirement)
'In case we need it later' is a speculative-abstraction red flag
Build it when the second SDK becomes an actual requirement, not before

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly names the real triggers that would justify it
